title: Coming of age
hookLine: at thirteen for boys, and twelve or thirteen for girls, one becomes responsible for the commandments

cards: A question with a surprising answer. A Jewish boy turns thirteen. His family has no money for a party, no time to prepare, and the synagogue is closed that week for repairs.
No speech. No DJ. No one even remembers it's his birthday until dinner.
Is he bar mitzvah? Yes. Fully.
The day he turns thirteen, by Jewish law, it has already happened. The ceremony people picture celebrates something that comes with the calendar; it doesn't create it.

teach.b: Bar mitzvah. A son of the commandment; for a girl, bat mitzvah, a daughter of the commandment. First, the age.
Judah ben Tema's map of a life in Pirkei Avot, the one that opened this block, has a stage that reads: at thirteen, for the commandments.

For girls, the Mishnah treats twelve as the age of adulthood, and in Orthodox communities a girl becomes bat mitzvah at twelve; in some other communities, the celebration comes at thirteen, like a boy's.
Before this, a child is taught and encouraged, and parents carry the responsibility. After this, the young person carries it.
Keeping Shabbat, fasting on Yom Kippur, counting in a prayer quorum, in communities that count them: these now belong to them.
The word mitzvah means commandment; to be its son or daughter is to be the one it's addressed to.
Third, the father's line. Traditionally, when a son becomes bar mitzvah, the father says a short blessing thanking God for releasing him from responsibility for this one's deeds. It can sound cold.

Read another way, it's a handover, out loud: from today, your choices are yours. The blessing comes from a midrash on Jacob and Esau, twins who walked the same road until thirteen and then went their separate ways.

teach.h: THE PARTY IS NOT THE POINT.
teach.b: Fourth, the party. Celebrations have grown large in some places, and they can be joyful. But as day six put it, it's not just a party.
The point is a young person standing up, responsible now.

how: Jews become bar or bat mitzvah by age: thirteen for boys, and twelve or thirteen for girls depending on the community. Many mark it with a synagogue ceremony and a celebration, though the status comes with the age itself.

o: a party a family throws for a boy's birthday
the first time a boy reads a Hebrew letter
son of the commandment: responsible at thirteen

s: without a ceremony, a boy never becomes bar mitzvah
it comes with the age; the ceremony celebrates it.
in Orthodox communities, a girl often becomes bat mitzvah at twelve
the Mishnah treats twelve as a girl's age of adulthood.
mitzvah means a good deed and nothing more
mitzvah means commandment; a bar mitzvah is the one it's now addressed to.

games.q: you've just turned thirteen. no party, no ceremony, no one has even remembered yet. are you bar mitzvah?
o: no, not until there's a ceremony.
yes, it comes with the age.
only after you read from the Torah.
games.why: by Jewish law it has already happened; the ceremony celebrates what the calendar brought.

practice: Think back to a moment someone handed you something for good, a key, a job, a person to care for, a decision now yours, and notice whether they said it out loud or it just happened.

Then name one responsibility you carry today that's fully yours, that no one else will pick up if you don't, and hold it without judging how well you carry it. If you pray, ask for strength to carry it.

wordCard.voice: Bar mitzvah. Son of the commandment, and bat mitzvah, daughter of the commandment: the age when responsibility passes from parent to child. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic bar, son, with Hebrew mitzvah, commandment.

carryVoice: Your line: responsible now. A thirteenth birthday, and a handover said out loud. That's the day.
